findings.issue_text: [High/security] `canManage()` grants management to callers with only global `view` permission, allowing view-only principals to create groups and satisfy global manage checks.

[High/bug] `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` uses the authorization resource ID instead of the Keycloak group ID for permission lookup and returned IDs, causing scoped group-member permissions to mis-constrain or fail group-based user listings.
[Medium/bug] Global all-groups permissions are ignored for a group once any resource-specific policy exists, so global permissions such as manage-all-groups do not provide the intended fallback.

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/bug] Global all-groups permissions are ignored for a group once any resource-specific policy exists, so global permissions such as manage-all-groups do not provide the intended fallback.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(), when groupId is null OR when the resource is not found, it falls back to checking the resource type resource (all-groups). The code explicitly handles this: 'if (resource == null) { resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) }'. The finding claims global permissions are ignored once resource-specific policies exist, but the code shows that when checking a specific group, if no resource exists for that group, it falls back to the type-level resource. The logic appears correct - it checks for specific resource first, then falls back to type-level. The finding misreads how the permission evaluation works.
